title: To rinse or not to rinse: jars, tins and tubs
description: Recycling containers do not need to be spotless, but a quick rinse protects the rest of the load and your kitchen too.

body.heading: Clean enough is the standard
paragraphs: Sorting plants ask for containers that are empty and reasonably clean, not washed like dinner dishes. A quick rinse or a wipe with used dishwater removes the food residue that causes smells and attracts pests, and that is enough.
A jar with a smear of jam is fine. A tub still holding half its soup is not, because that food ends up smeared across paper and cardboard that then cannot be recycled.

body.heading: Rinse without wasting water
paragraphs: Use the end of the washing-up water, or rinse several containers together in a small amount of water rather than running each under a hot tap. The goal is clean recycling without undoing the good with a flood of heated water.

Greasy pizza boxes and takeaway trays are a special case: the cardboard fibres absorb oil and cannot be separated, so most services ask for them in general waste or food-waste composting instead. Clean sections can sometimes be torn off and recycled.

body.heading: Lids, labels and pumps
paragraphs: Labels can stay on; sorting plants handle them. Metal lids can usually go in the bin loose or placed inside the can, but rules differ, so check your local list once.
Pump and spray tops are mixed materials and are often not accepted, while the bottle beneath them is. Removing the top takes a second and keeps a good bottle from being rejected with a bad lid.

takeaway: Aim for empty and rinsed, not sparkling, and use leftover dishwater so the rinse itself wastes nothing.
